title: Rules for discernment
hook: in desolation, don't make big changes

segments.voice: Yesterday, consolation and desolation. Your line was which way am I drifting? At noon or at night, which way was the arrow pointing? Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

It's late, the house is quiet, and everything feels wrong. The job seems pointless. The friendship seems over. Faith feels hollow. And in that mood a decision shows up, looking very clear: quit, send the message, walk away. In the morning, with coffee and some light through the window, the same choice can look very different. Ignatius of Loyola wrote a rule for exactly that night. It's short enough to remember half asleep, and it comes out of yesterday's two words. Today: rules for discernment.

Discernment means sorting: telling one thing from another. The first letter of John puts it this way in the King James: "Beloved, believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God." Try them. Test them. Ignatius' rules are a field guide for that testing, and today rests on the fifth. In time of desolation, he says, never make a change. Stay firm in what you decided before the darkness came, in the calm or in consolation. His reason is plain. In desolation, the voice giving advice isn't a good counselor. A decision made in that fog tends to follow the fog. But he doesn't say do nothing. His next rule says push back against the desolation itself: pray a little more, think it through, look honestly at what's happening, do some small thing against the mood. Hold the course. Change your effort, not your plans. Then he gives advice for the bright days too. In consolation, think ahead to how you'll be when it passes, and store up strength for then. And stay humble, remembering how little you could manage in the low times. He also offers a picture of how temptation works: like a commander who studies a fortress and attacks where the wall is weakest. Each person's weak place is different, and knowing your own is part of keeping watch. None of this means desolation is failure, or that every hard feeling is an enemy. It means some choices deserve daylight. The big ones especially: the job, the move, the vow.

Here's the practice: postpone one decision till calm. Settle and breathe. Ask whether there's a choice you've been tempted to make in a low or rattled moment. A message to send. Something to quit. A purchase. A door to slam. Don't decide anything now. Just set it down, gently, on a shelf for a calmer day. Notice what it's like to leave it there. If you pray, you can bring it to God and ask for light. The bell holds the time.
Discernment. Sorting the movements inside, testing which pull is which, and choosing in the light.
Your line: never decide in the dark. Today, if something big comes up while you're low, write it down and give it till tomorrow. Day one thousand one hundred forty-seven.

howItsDone: Ignatian retreat guides and spiritual directors teach the rules for discernment of spirits, and people use them when weighing decisions, often waiting to choose until desolation has passed.

fork.setup: you're in desolation. everything feels hollow, and quitting a commitment suddenly looks obvious. what does Ignatius' fifth rule say?
options: act now, while it feels clear.
make no change; hold to what you decided in calm, and push back on the mood.
wait, and do nothing at all.
fork.reveal: never make a change in desolation, he says, but don't just sit there either: pray more, look honestly, act against the mood.

trapdoor: what you thought: discernment is a fancy word for making up your mind.
what it means: sorting the pulls inside, and refusing to make big changes in the dark.
what a scholar hears: the fifth rule pairs with the sixth: no change of plans, but a change of effort against the desolation.

notes: Paraphrases First Week rules: 5 (in desolation never make a change; stay firm in the resolution of before), 6 (change oneself intensely against desolation: more prayer, meditation, examination, some fitting penance; 'do some small thing against the mood' softens 'penance'), 10–11 (in consolation think how one will be in desolation, store up strength, humble oneself), 14 (the commander attacking the weakest point). Confirm numbering and wording.
1 John 4:1 quoted in part; the verse continues 'because many false prophets are gone out into the world.'
